cards.front: What are the four Coffman conditions required for deadlock to occur?
cards.back: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four must hold simultaneously.

cards.front: Define the mutual exclusion condition for deadlock.
cards.back: At least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode; only one process may use it at a time.

cards.front: Explain the hold-and-wait condition with a brief example.
cards.back:
A process holding at least one resource is waiting to acquire additional resources already held by other processes.
Example: P1 holds R1 and waits for R2; P2 holds R2 and waits for R1.

cards.front: Define the no-preemption condition for deadlock.
cards.back: Resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process; they can only be released voluntarily by the holding process after it has finished using them.

cards.front: Describe the circular-wait condition and its graph representation.
cards.back: A set of processes {P0, P1, …, Pn} exists such that P0 waits for a resource held by P1, P1 waits for one held by P2, …, Pn waits for one held by P0. In the resource-allocation graph this forms a cycle.

cards.front: Why must all four Coffman conditions be present simultaneously for deadlock?
cards.back: Each condition eliminates a necessary escape route: mutual exclusion prevents sharing, hold-and-wait prevents releasing while acquiring, no-preemption prevents forced release, and circular wait closes the only remaining scheduling loop. Removing any one breaks the deadlock possibility.

cards.front: How can the circular-wait condition be prevented by resource ordering?
cards.back: Impose a total ordering on resource types and require every process to request resources in strictly increasing order. This makes a cycle impossible.
